speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the restricted inflow of workers to Singapore has affected companies in Singapore and their ability and capacity to meet business commitments; and (b) what measures are being considered to mitigate the impact on companies and the products and services they provide to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) from November 2020 to April 2021, how many In-Principle Approvals (IPA) and successful Entry Passes respectively have been granted to Work Permit and S Pass applicants from the construction, marine and process sectors on a monthly basis; and (b) whether the Ministry will expand the list of source countries from where companies in these sectors can employ foreign workers to work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the contraction in total employment of non-residents by 181,500 throughout 2020 is also matched by a decline in the total population of non-residents in Singapore in the same period; (b) what are the reasons why non-residents who lose their jobs in Singapore may not be required to leave immediately; (c) how many non-residents who lost their jobs in 2020 have been allowed to remain in Singapore; and (d) how many non-residents who lost their jobs in 2020 have been re-employed in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Pritam Singh asked about the restricted inflow of workers and what we are doing to support businesses affected by these restrictions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Businesses have, indeed, been affected, quite badly, particularly with the Construction, Marine Shipyard and Process (CMP) sectors being the hardest hit as they rely heavily on migrant workers for jobs that few locals would want to work in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are very mindful of the manpower crunch that these firms face today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Besides providing financial relief to help them, we are also taking steps to alleviate the manpower shortage.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, restrictions on inflow of workers from higher risk countries is likely to persist for some time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is as the size of the inflow coming in has to be reduced when the COVID-19 situation deteriorates in these source countries from where they come from, and we can only increase these inflows when the situation in these home countries improve.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers can make use of these rebates to bring in workers from alternative sources, such as China, where the workers are generally higher skilled and, at the same time, command higher wages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and Building and Construction Authority (BCA) also recently announced a temporary scheme to allow these new Work Permit holders from China to obtain their skills certification in Singapore, since some of the Overseas Testing Centres in China have not resumed operations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: BCA and the Economic Development Board will continue to engage firms and we will continue to review if additional measures are needed to help the CMP sectors through this crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the meantime, we encourage businesses to retain their existing migrant workers and tap on other workers that are already here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked if the non-resident employment decline in 2020 of 181,500 was matched by the decline in total population of non-residents within the same period.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When a work pass expires or is cancelled, we typically require the worker to leave Singapore in two to four weeks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This depends, of course, on the pass type.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Time is given for the employer to arrange repatriation and also for the worker to settle his or her own personal affairs, such as closure of bank accounts and termination of leases.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Each year, about 30% of all work pass holders do not continue employment with their original employer and have their passes expired or cancelled.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the work pass holder is able to find new employment before repatriation, there is no reason for us to purposefully force this worker to return to his home country, for him to incur additional recruitment fees from overseas employment agents, to undergo additional COVID-19 testing and, on return to Singapore, to serve up to 21 days Stay-Home Notice (SHN).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Furthermore, making the worker do this unnecessary round-trip would increase the risk of him returning with a COVID-19 infection.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the other hand, however, if the work pass holder does not find new employment before the deadline, we ensure that his former employer will fulfil its obligation to successfully repatriate the worker.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we had insisted that the worker had to leave Singapore even though he has already found an employer, we would have had to allow the entry of nearly double the number of workers last year, and this would further strain our SHN facilities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, the alternative would be to compound further the manpower difficulties faced by businesses, as what the hon Member of Parliament Ms Jessica Tan and also Mr Pritam Singh have highlighted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have heard about anecdotes of companies applying for entry permits for their workers 30, 40, sometimes almost 50 times for one In-Principle Approval (IPA).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It sounds like a large number; and, of course, the companies get frustrated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, there is also an acknowledgement that the Government has to control the COVID-19 situation as best it can.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it is a very fine balancing act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, I have three supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand MOM extends it one time as a given.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That means if the IPA is for three months for the Work Permit holder, MOM will extend it automatically.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question is: would MOM be amenable to reimburse IPA application fees if, for whatever reason, the applying company decides, "Look, I don't think it is possible to continue with this uncertainty".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, would MOM consider reimbursing the IPA cost if the entry pass just does not come through?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The third question pertains to the second part of my two-part PQ.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some contractors have suggested non-traditional source countries like Vietnam as a potential source for workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I know there is a long tail to this, it is not a case of just getting a person from any country; there is a whole process of training, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would this be something the Ministry would look into?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the IPA, the In-Principle Approvals, and the entry approvals or the final entry approvals, there are actually two separate independent processes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Obviously, we do receive and we do give out a lot more IPAs than the entry approvals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of the key challenges of this pandemic is the fact that the situation is extremely fluid and dynamic.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Why do I say it is fluid and dynamic?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because of the source countries where our workers come from, the situation back in many of these source countries – I think you have seen in the news – what we are seeing are successive waves of infection.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, as a result of that, you find that at the point of application of the IPA, as long as it fulfils the requirements of what we have in terms of what is needed for them to come in, we grant the approval.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But to regulate the control in terms of the onboarding of these migrant workers coming into Singapore, we do it via the entry approval route.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And that is dependent on the risk quota which we are able to accept.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is also a function of certain Not-to-Land (NTL) Restrictions, for instance, that the MTF decides and, at the same time, also a function of how many of these SHN facilities we have available.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier on in the year, we announced the set-up of the Migrant Worker Onboarding Centre, which is a one-stop centre to screen all of them, so as to make sure that it is safe before they go into the community.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is also a function of the number of beds that we have.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because of that, you find that the IPAs usually will far exceed the number of actual entry approvals coming into Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that part of it is cleared up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's point about whether we can grant an extension – depending on the different Pass types, whether it is EP, S Pass and Work Permit – to the IPAs with different lengths of validity, today, the default answer to the point about the renewals and the automatic extension of IPAs – that is what we are now doing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, we are seeing that because of the backlog of cases – that backlog has increased significantly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As a result, even if you allow for an automatic extension of that IPA, it does not make sense because that extension is going to go months ahead without any certainty as to whether, ultimately, we can grant the entry approvals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because if it is too long again in the future, it does not make sense.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are trying to find a more nuanced way, so that we can make it a lot easier.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, obviously, this would take time because there are also language and cultural issues.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are things that we have to take into consideration.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With regard to the industries, I know that the marine shipyard, construction and process industries have been most impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I am also concerned about the small and medium enterprises or SMEs in terms of the services and their ability to continue to operate outside of these industries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are some jobs – especially for Work Permit holders – that many of these SMEs are facing difficulty in terms of the ability to renew the Work Permits for, as well as to get sufficient workers for jobs that they are finding hard to fill, even as they look at alternative sources in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, my question to the Minister is, in terms of the extensions for existing Work Permit holders or S Passes for workers in Singapore, can that be considered, especially for the SMEs, because one or two workers make a big difference for them in terms of their ability to continue to operate?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, at this particular point in time, we are in crisis mode.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, all the appeals that come from all sectors, we will consider and we will review them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is the reassurance that we can give.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of the appeals to grant extensions, we should also take note of the tremendous slew of measures that the Government has put forth to support SMEs – in the form of Job Support Scheme, the Job Growth Incentive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, we have got quite a number of other schemes to try and support our entire economy and our industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is not just one aspect or measure to help the SMEs only.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Tan will be comforted to know that the Government has also put in a very comprehensive set of measures to help support them as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister confirmed that last year, there was a contraction of about 180,000 in non-resident employment and there was also an outflow of these people from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, there is also a number that said that there is a shortage of about 60,000 workers in the CMP sectors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, can I confirm whether there has been a re-entry of 130,000 foreign workers into our country in the last few months?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, that represents a net outflow of 3,200 per month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, if you add both the CMP sector plus the services sector, the net outflow is about 5,600 per month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We could not sustain that inflow because of the fact that – as I have said – the situation is very dynamic and very fluid.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The moment in any of these source countries the infection rates go up, we would have to throttle the number again.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that gives Mr Leong a sense of how acutely or how grave the shortage of workers is today in our industry.
